observations.observedDetails: Title identifies Lecture 37, Obstacle Avoidance.
Objectives span grid graphs, A* g/h/f, local sensors, Bug0/1/2, VFH reduction and comparison.
Contents list A* example, avoidance introduction, Bug algorithms, VFH and manipulators.
Actual 5x5 grid: top-left three cells and column2 rows1 through3 blocked; start(4,4), goal(2,0); minimum f=g+h frontier principle.
Coordinates index rows and columns from zero; indices bounded by M and N despite generic x/y terminology.
Binary occupancy 0 free/1 obstacle; free cells form vertices; cardinal cost1 and diagonal sqrt2 approximately1.4.
Displayed g costs imply no corner cutting: goal5.4, row3col1=4, row4col1=3, start0; use rounded1.4 to reproduce displayed figures.
Displayed h ignores walls using octile costs: goal0 and start4.8; obstacles do not increase the heuristic.
Combined g/h diagram changes start g to1 despite previous page0; green route passes bottom row to column1 then row3col1 then goal. This is an actual source discrepancy.
New obstacle at(3,1) blocks the previous path; left-bottom detour costs6. This example is compatible with rerunning global A* after a map update.

Exteroceptive sensing examples include sonar, LiDAR, IR and camera; figures show RPLIDAR range display and Pi Camera semantic detections. Printed product specifications are source claims, not independently verified specifications.
Local avoidance uses recent readings alongside global planning; goal, speed/kinematics, sensor capabilities and collision risk are named objectives. Optimality wording is not a general proof.
Actual red avoidance trajectory bends around a cylinder then returns to the dashed desired global direction; decision uses sensing and relative goal.
Bug variants use different sensors and retained information; perimeter following keeps a chosen obstacle side, not necessarily repeated same-direction turns.
Bug0 alternates go-to-goal and boundary following until goal direction clears; diagram leaves a curved obstacle. No traversed-path memory does not mean no instantaneous state.
Bug0 concave trap diagram shows cycling and incompleteness even though a route can exist; dotted trajectory folds around the obstacle.
Bug1 surveys the complete boundary, records closest-to-goal departure and returns by shorter boundary arc; H1/L1 and H2/L2 label hits/departures.
Bug1 completeness is ideal-model scoped; full boundary travel can be inefficient. Concave-trap illustration contrasts Bug0.
Bug2 returns to the original start-goal line at a point strictly closer than the hit, with goal-seek and wall-follow modes. H1/L1,H2/L2 lie on fixed dashed line.
Bug2 completeness and typical efficiency are qualified by model and geometry; source calls momentum kinematics and oversimplifies sensing memory.
VFH accumulates recent readings into a local map; robot arc around obstacle illustrates smoothing. Source contrast with purely reactive Bugs must not erase retained hit/line information.
Pipeline is 2D certainty grid to 1D polar density to steering; source calls certainty probabilities without specifying calibration.
Robot-centered active region updates while moving; light/free and dark/likely occupied grid figure; certainty increments near measured ranges. Pose registration is needed for temporal fusion.
Histogram alpha runs about -180 to180 degrees; central high peak indicates obstacle density, not range or commanded steering. Threshold above/below stated, equality omitted.
Valleys are contiguous free sectors; wide openings provide interior/goal-biased candidates, narrow openings center; absent goal-facing valley permits detour, not necessarily all directions blocked.

Cost weights target, current heading and previous direction errors; larger a favors goal, larger c favors smoothness. Diagram lower-right45 degree label conflicts with standard circular axis ordering; do not infer precise numerical geometry from it.
VFH+ width and turning-radius masking shown by a left blocked region expanding in masked histogram. Short-lookahead attribution requires distinction from VFH* explicit search.

Table: Bug instantaneous sensing, low robustness, no kinematics, Bug1/2 completeness, low cost/simple prototypes; VFH accumulated sensing, higher robustness,VFH+kinematics,no completeness guarantee,moderate cost/noisy sonar-LiDAR robots. Qualitative not universal measured claims.
Whole manipulator links can collide, including self-collision; 3D workspace and many independent joints make configuration search higher dimensional.

Actual configuration panel has theta1 horizontal and theta2 vertical, shaded C-obstacle, red current point outside. Workspace-to-C-space arrow labeled forward kinematics is reversed relative to true joint-to-geometry mapping. All-angle description assumes revolute coordinates.
Artificial field diagram: red outward obstacle arrows, blue inward goal arrows, black resultant motion. Computational forces need a suitable controller rather than being literal external forces.

Attractive pull increases with separation in the described field; repulsion acts within an influence radius; every relevant link receives obstacle effects; total field sums one attraction and multiple repulsions.
Dimensionality, non-goal local minima, self-collision, dynamic obstacles and whole-arm checks are all listed. Moving obstacles require updating the forbidden configuration set.
CNNs classify/segment image obstacles; learned thresholds/costs can replace hand tuning. Reference to a,b,c as potential weights does not match earlier angular steering-cost definition.

RL learns reward-shaped policies; mobile steering/velocity versus arm joint-angle/torque commands use different action spaces. Claimed superiority or escape from local minima is not a universal guarantee.
Summary contrasts global A*, local avoidance, Bug, VFH/VFH+ and every-link arm avoidance; known-static-map shorthand does not prohibit replanning after changes.
Reference-only slide names Siegwart and Nourbakhsh, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots.
Thank-you slide, no additional examinable content.
